Headliner Big Pete Pearson brings his five-piece band, Tucson’s Bad News Blues Band makes a rare northern appearance, and Big Daddy D and the Dynamites round out the night. A strong Saturday-night ticket for blues lovers and Valley Dwellers alike. | Show Low Film Festival — festival weekend, Oct. 16–18, WME Village 8, 1501 W White Mountain Blvd, Pinetop-Lakeside. Now in its eighth year, this White Mountains festival screens its top independent films on the big screens, from shorts to features and documentaries. Filmmakers attend in person, with workshops across the weekend, and day passes and single-block tickets are on sale. Note the films are not yet rated, and the festival itself says it is not suggested for children. | Cowboy Prom for a Cause — 5:30–8:30 PM, gates 5 PM, 3092 Jacks Rd, Pinetop-Lakeside. A benefit country night with live music from Heber Ridge, dancing, barbecue, and raffle and auction items, White Mountains style. Listings say proceeds support the Johnson family as they face a stage-three cancer diagnosis while raising two children. Admission is listed at $35 per person or $65 per couple. Boots and hats welcome — verify tickets on the event page before going.

[week Wed, Oct. 21] Lunch & Learn: Google Business Profile & the Value of Reviews — Payson Unified School District, 902 W Main St, Payson. A midday learning session for local business owners on how a Google Business Profile and honest customer reviews bring travelers through the door. Most useful to hosts, shopkeepers, and guides who serve Hearth guests across Rim Country. It is listed for Wednesday, Oct. 21 in Payson’s event roundups. Check the Chamber calendar for the start time and RSVP.

[merchant name] Carpenter’s Wife Antiques

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] A proper general-goods trader’s shop for the Hold: thirteen rooms packed to the ceiling with antique furniture, home decor, collectibles, boutique clothing, antique books, candles, and Western and Native pieces, plus local jams and honey — and a backyard of rust-and-relics besides. [merchant review_src] Phyllis N. on Yelp (via Roadtrippers)

[tale title] The Great Kite Trial

[tale] Turdas dawned sunny with a brisk wind worrying the pines, and Gus (a friendly orc baker) decided his new diamond kite ought to be tested before lunch, not after. “Wind waits for no pie,” he said, which Mabel (a wood elf) noted was not a saying.

Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) towed the kite aloft and, thanks to the famous kink in his tail, flew his usual zigzag — so the kite wrote delighted loops over the clearing while the string wound itself twice around Gus’s hat. Henny (the Hearth’s chicken) took charge of the string end with unbothered professionalism, marching backward one solemn step at a time, paying out line like a harbormaster.

When a gust finally set the kite down — gently, in Mabel’s herb garden, atop the sage — nobody scolded anybody. Gus declared the trial a triumph, Flurry took a bow mid-air and landed in a leaf drift, and Henny kept the string. She appears to own a kite now.

[tale image caption] Flurry tows, Henny holds the line, and Gus calls it a triumph.

[weather] Sunny and clear high 60 low 44 rain 0% sunrise 6:30 AM sunset 5:51 PM tomorrow Sunny, 67/52

[weather_caption] Gandy basks half-asleep in the sun while Maevy chases a butterfly clean off the deck.

[today Payson] Baby Story Time at the Payson Public Library — 10:30 AM, 328 N McLane Rd. The library celebrates its youngest readers with board books and songs, in a gentle gathering made for babies and their grown-ups. It is a sweet first mead-hall for the Hold’s smallest travelers, and a fine way to meet other young families. No registration is needed — just come and sing along. | Tai-Chi at the Payson Public Library — 9 AM, 328 N McLane Rd. Start the sunny Middas with slow, deliberate movement among friends at the library’s regular Wednesday Tai-Chi gathering. [week Thu, Oct. 15] A Band Called Honalee — 7 PM, 301 S McLane Rd, Payson. This modern-day folk trio relives the timeless magic of Peter, Paul & Mary, bringing classics the whole hall knows by heart to life with stirring vocal harmonies. The show also honors Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and other legends of the age. A warm Turdas evening of songs carried the way traveling bards once carried news between holds. | Gary Allan — 7:30 PM, Findlay Toyota Center, Prescott Valley. PINE Strawberry Fuel Reduction calls hikers, bikers, runners, and neighbors to clear brush, move rocks, and shape trails that will serve the Hold for years, while opening better access routes for firefighters. Tools are provided; bring water, gloves, and your good will. Email trails@psfuelreduction.org to volunteer.

[merchant name] Udderly Divine

[merchant town] Camp Verde

[merchant blurb] In Camp Verde’s 1915 Historic Dance Hall on Main Street, this family-owned bakery and coffee shop serves breakfast, lunch, homemade baked goods, take-and-bake meals, and a 15-flavor ice-cream parlor besides. The signature wonder is the towering cinnamon roll — the closest thing in any Hold to a true Skyrim sweet roll, kept lofty, one suspects, by a minor levitation charm in the oven. Hearty biscuits and gravy and Theresa’s legendary bread pudding round out the feast.

[merchant review] Everything is delicious!

[merchant review_src] Facebook review

[merchant why] Because no traveler should pass Camp Verde without tasting a cinnamon roll tall enough to need its own saga — warm, sweet, and gone too soon.

[tale title] The Great Leaf-Pile Leap

[tale] Middas dawned sunny and clear, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) declared the fallen leaves in the Hearth clearing wasted lying flat. By mid-morning he had raked them into a pile taller than Gus’s pie rack, and announced the first Great Leaf-Pile Leap, with himself as first leaper and only judge.

Earl (an elk) declined to leap. Earl agreed, with great dignity, to stand nearby and look official. This was a mistake. Jethro’s leap scattered half the pile straight over him, and for a long minute the clearing held nothing of Earl but two enormous antlers rising out of the leaves like a sunken ship’s masts.

Henny (the Hearth’s chicken) marched out of the pile wearing a crown of oak leaves she had not been wearing when she went in, and refused to explain it. Mabel (a wood elf) sighed, fetched Earl a path out with her rake, and ruled the contest a tie.

Jethro is already raking tomorrow’s pile. Earl is standing much farther away.

[tale image caption] Jethro leaps, Earl vanishes to the antlers, and Henny emerges crowned.

[tale title] The Rain-Tin Orchestra

[tale] Tirdas dawned wet, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) took it into his head that the rain was wasted falling unheard. By breakfast he had lined the Hearth’s deck rail with every vessel he could borrow — Gus’s pie tins, Mabel’s watering cans, and one dented old helmet — each set to catch the rain and sing its own small note.

Henny (the Hearth’s chicken) appointed herself conductor, as is her right. She mounted an upturned bucket, shook the rain off her comb, and flapped the whole orchestra into time, while the tins went plink, the cans went plonk, and the helmet, being deep, went bong at moments nobody expected.

Earl (an elk) wanted no part of the concert. He settled under the eaves for a dignified nap, but one pie tin had landed on his antlers, and it dripped — drip — drip — square between his eyes. Mabel (a wood elf) sighed, moved the tin two inches, and the drip fell harmless on the deck boards.

Earl slept the whole performance through. Jethro calls it his finest review.

[tale image caption] Henny conducts, the tins play, and Earl endures his one-tin serenade.

headline: Rain Soaks the Rim as Art, Music & Hula Fill the Week
greeting: PAYSON — Hail, good neighbor, and mind the puddles! Morndas has thrown open the very floodgates over the Mogollon Rim, with rain drumming the pines all day and a Flood Watch standing till five o'clock — a fine day for the mead hall, the museum shelf, and watching Gandy glare at the sky from the dry boards. The week ahead dries out and dresses up: the Payson Art League's ARToberFest fills the Mazatzal Casino Event Center Friday through Sunday, Sedona's Plein Air Festival sets up its easels across the red rocks, Camp Verde sways to Hawaiian hula, and Sunday brings a parade of costumed hounds to Tlaquepaque. [headline] Rain Soaks the Rim as Art, Music & Hula Fill the Week

[dateline] Monday, October 12, 2026

[lead] PAYSON — Hail, good neighbor, and mind the puddles! Morndas has thrown open the very floodgates over the Mogollon Rim, with rain drumming the pines all day and a Flood Watch standing till five o'clock — a fine day for the mead hall, the museum shelf, and watching Gandy glare at the sky from the dry boards. The week ahead dries out and dresses up: the Payson Art League's ARToberFest fills the Mazatzal Casino Event Center Friday through Sunday, Sedona's Plein Air Festival sets up its easels across the red rocks, Camp Verde sways to Hawaiian hula, and Sunday brings a parade of costumed hounds to Tlaquepaque. By the Nine, keep your cloak handy today and your dancing shoes ready for the weekend.

[hero_caption] The week ahead paints itself: ARToberFest in Payson, easels up across Sedona, and fall festivals under the Rim.

[weather] Rain — Flood Watch until 5 PM high 59 low 52 rain 80% (~0.5 in.) sunrise 6:28 AM sunset 5:54 PM tomorrow Morning rain, then partly cloudy, 59/44

[weather_caption] Gandy guards the dry boards while Maevy tries to catch the sky.

[weather_overheard] Overheard Last Night — A soaked traveler asked the barkeep when the rain would let up. The barkeep only shrugged: “Aye — the Watch runs till five, but the pines will believe it when they see it.”

[today Pine-Strawberry] Open Mic Night: Music with a Purpose — 4–7 PM at THAT Brewery & Pub, 3270 N AZ-87, Pine. The community open mic returns on its every-other-Monday rhythm, hosted this season by the Pine-Strawberry Fuel Reduction crew, with all tips going to forest-protection work. Seasoned pickers, first-time singers, poets, and storytellers all take the little stage — or just claim a pint and a bench and let the neighbors entertain you. A warm, wood-stove sort of evening; the rain on the roof only improves it.

[today Prescott] Prescott History Tour — 10 AM–noon, departing downtown Prescott. A two-hour guided walk through the old territorial capital's most storied streets, from Whiskey Row's saloons to the Victorian mansions of Nob Hill, led by guides who know every governor and ghost. Book ahead at freakyfoottours.com. A fine outing for history-curious guests — and the rain gives Whiskey Row a properly atmospheric gleam. | Fall Break Nature Camp — Monday through Friday, 8 AM–4 PM, Highlands Center for Natural History, 1375 S Walker Rd. A fully outdoor week of hiking, games, science investigations, and journaling on Prescott National Forest trails, for ages 6–10. $250 for members, $300 for non-members. (The Seedlings half-day track for little ones is full, with a waitlist.) | Fall Zoo Camp — Monday through Friday, 8:30 AM–3 PM, Heritage Park Zoological Sanctuary, 1403 Heritage Park Rd. Ages 6–12 get hands-on animal time, behind-the-scenes visits, wildlife games, crafts, and investigations at Prescott's hometown zoo. $250 for members, $300 for non-members. A grand week for young naturalists.

[week Tuesday, Oct. 13] Trail Day Volunteer Build — 7 AM–noon, off AZ-87 just before Pine. The Pine-Strawberry Fuel Reduction crew calls hikers, bikers, runners, and forest-lovers to clear brush, move rock, and shape new trail that doubles as firefighter access. No experience needed and tools are provided — bring water, gloves, and sturdy boots, and RSVP to trails@psfuelreduction.org for the meeting spot. Honest work under tall pines, and the best breakfast appetite you'll earn all week.

[week Thursday, Oct. 15] A Band Called Honalee — 7 PM, Payson High School Auditorium, 301 S McLane Rd. A modern folk trio channeling Peter, Paul & Mary — “Leaving on a Jet Plane,” “Blowin' in the Wind,” “Puff the Magic Dragon” — in close three-part harmony, with nods to Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and the Mamas & the Papas. Thirty-odd locals have already flagged they're going. A gentle, sing-along sort of evening for folk hearts. | Gary Allan with Julie Eddy — 7:30 PM, Findlay Toyota Center, 3201 N Main St, Prescott Valley. The country hitmaker behind “Man to Man” and “Every Storm (Runs Out of Rain)” brings his raspy honky-tonk show to the region's big arena. The week's biggest-ticket concert — third-party listings show seats from about $64. A proper arena night out under the Rim.

[week Friday, Oct. 16] ARToberFest — Friday through Sunday, Mazatzal Casino Event Center. The Payson Art League's annual fine art and fine craft show and sale gathers the Hold's artists all in one hall, with the Payson Jazz Trio playing and an art raffle benefiting local school art programs. Come to browse or come to buy — the raffle alone is worth the trip, and the whole weekend hums. | 22nd Annual Sedona Plein Air Festival — Friday through Oct. 24, Sedona Arts Center, 15 Art Barn Rd, plus painting sites across Sedona and the Verde Valley. One of the West's oldest plein air festivals: dozens of master artists painting the red rocks outdoors, with free public demonstrations and paint-outs all week long. Free to watch the artists work; the grand sale closes the festival Oct. 24.

[week Saturday, Oct. 17] Fest of Fall — Saturday, Posse Grounds Park, 525 Posse Ground Rd (the city lists 11 AM–5 PM). Sedona's family fall celebration: food trucks, local brews, live music, craft and nonprofit vendors, pickleball and cornhole tournaments, a kids' zone with pumpkin carving, skate jam, and photo booth. Pair it with the morning's Pumpkin Splash at the community pool (11 AM–1 PM, $5 — pick your pumpkin right out of the water). Free, low-waste, and made for lingering. | 21st Annual Ho'ike — Hula Exhibition — Doors 12:30 PM, show 1 PM, Phillip England Center for the Performing Arts, 280 Camp Lincoln Rd, Camp Verde. Authentic Hawaiian hula, music, and culture in the Verde Valley: a scholar's presentation on ancient hula instruments opens the show, followed by modern hula, a 50-50 raffle, island goods, and a silent auction of Hawaiian art. Proceeds benefit Aloha 'Aina O Hawai'i. The most transporting afternoon of the week.

[week Sunday, Oct. 18] Howl-O-Ween Dog Costume Parade — 10 AM–noon (check-in 9–9:30 AM), Tlaquepaque Arts & Shopping Village, 336 SR-179, Sedona. The 6th annual parade of costumed canines, from Calle Independencia to Tlaquepaque North — $20 per dog, with proceeds to the Humane Society of Sedona. Costume contests carry $100 prizes (Doggone Cutest, Craziest Canine, and the group Leaders of the Pack), judged by the mayor-elect himself. Even dogless, it's the happiest two hours in the Verde Valley.

[merchant name] Western Village

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] Twenty-five thousand square feet of treasure on the Beeline — antiques, fine art, and high-end jewelry, plus a glittering back wing of gems, rocks, and minerals that would make a dragon weep with envy. Native American artifacts, cowboy memorabilia, vintage books, taxidermy, and room after room of frontier curiosities. It could pass for a museum, except here you're allowed to take the exhibits home.

[merchant review] A very nice western store. Wonderful gems and jewelry items. All genuine.

[merchant review_src] TripAdvisor

[merchant why] Because no guest should leave the Rim without one good treasure-hunting morning — and this is the grandest trove in the Hold.

[merchant visit] 1104 S Beeline Hwy, Payson — open daily 10 AM–5 PM, closed Tuesdays; (928) 474-3431; easy on the purse ($–$$). Good to know: pets are welcome, and there's layaway for the grand finds.

[merchant image caption] The gem counter at Western Village, where the dragon's-hoard glitters.

[tale title] The Great Trench Rescue

[tale] Morndas dawned with the sky wrung out over the Rim, and Mabel (a wood elf) stood in her herb garden watching her sage drown. “Trench,” she announced, the way a general declares war. “We dig a trench, or the thyme goes swimming.”

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) took this as a personal commission. He dropped to all fours and plowed a furrow down the middle of the garden with his whole enormous body, humming a digging song, while Earl (an elk) stood by in enormous dignity holding Mabel's plumb line in his antlers so she could sight the slope. “Left,” said Mabel. Earl leaned left. “Right.” Earl leaned right, and the plumb bob swung round and bopped him square on the nose.

Gus (a friendly orc) arrived with a tray of trench pies — “morale rations,” he rumbled softly — just as Henny (a plump red-combed chicken) declared the deepest puddle her personal pond and christened it with a splash.

By noon the garden drained sweet as a whistle. The single casualty: Jethro's trench ran a touch too true and drained Mabel's rain barrel clean through the fence boards. Jethro stared at the empty barrel, then up at the weeping sky, and said, “Well. The sky will fill it back.”

Mabel sighed like it was her job. “It had better,” she said. “It's on trench duty next.”

[tale image caption] Jethro plows the trench while Earl sights the slope and Henny christens the puddles.

headline: A Stormy Sundas: Quilts, Chili, and the Last Fair Day
greeting: PAYSON — Hail, travelers! Sundas dawned grey and growling over the Mogollon Rim.
text:
[headline] A Stormy Sundas: Quilts, Chili, and the Last Fair Day

[dateline] Sunday, October 11, 2026

[lead] PAYSON — Hail, travelers! Sundas dawned grey and growling over the Mogollon Rim, the storm drumming the pines while the Holds made merry indoors: today is the last day of the Rim Country Quilt Round-Up in Payson, the Fall & Antique Festival's chili cook-off in Pine, and Fort Verde Days' homecoming celebration down in Camp Verde. Keep an eye on the sky — a Flood Watch holds till Monday's small hours — and keep the week in your sights, for the days ahead bring trail-building, folk songs, the town council's gathering on Wednesday, and the Payson Art League's ARToberFest filling the weekend. By the Nine, there's no weather too wild for Rim Country doings.

[hero_caption] A market fair beneath the pines: quilts on the line, chili on the fire, and pumpkins by the antique stall.

[weather] Heavy thunderstorms — Flood Watch until Mon 5 AM; Wind Advisory 8 AM–8 PM high 61 low 54 rain 100% (~1.19 in.) sunrise 6:27 AM sunset 5:55 PM tomorrow Rain, 59/51

[weather_caption] Gandy keeps his grump dry under the eaves while Maevy conducts the rain.

[today Payson] Rim Country Quilt Round-Up — Last day today. The quilt guild's autumn gathering fills the Mazatzal Hotel & Casino Event Center with quilting classes and displays of fine stitchery — rows of finished quilts, demonstrations, and vendors for the fabric-minded. Wander the aisles for an hour or a day; quilters are the friendliest folk in the Hold. (Runs Friday through today, Sunday, Oct. 11.) | ACA Race #3 // Ubuntu Trail — The Arizona Cycling Association's scholastic mountain-bike series rolls into the Payson Event Center and Ubuntu Trail area today, with the first races off at 8 AM and awards late in the afternoon. Middle- and high-school racers from across the North Conference take on the course while families cheer from the sidelines. Come watch the future of Rim Country riding.

[today Pine-Strawberry] Annual Fall & Antique Festival — Last day today, 9 AM–4 PM at the Pine-Strawberry Community Center, 3886 N Hwy 87 in Pine. A chili cook-off, food and craft vendors, a pumpkin patch, and an antique show inside the Cultural Hall — the twin villages' autumn send-off in one stop. Come hungry; leave with something old. (Runs Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 10–11.)

[today Camp Verde] Fort Verde Days — Last day today of Camp Verde's big annual homecoming, the town's celebration of the frontier military post it grew up around. Sunday brings vendors, entertainment, and living-history events at Fort Verde State Historic Park, 646 S. 1st Street — admission free. Saturday's parade has passed, but the old camp's story carries the day. (Runs Friday through Sunday, Oct. 9–11.)

[today Sedona] Sedona Community Farmers Market — Sundays, now on winter hours: 11 AM–3 PM at the Wells Fargo parking lot, 2201 W SR 89A, weekly through May 30, 2027. Local growers, bakers, and makers set out their tables for the valley's regular Sunday trade. Worth the drive for the fresh bread alone. | Alternative Firing 1-Day Workshop with CJ Henderson — 10 AM at 15 Art Barn Rd. A hands-on day of pottery finishing techniques — raku-style alternative firings that coax fire-born color from the clay. All skill levels welcome; take home something the kiln gods smiled on.

[today Prescott] Prescott History Tour — 10 AM. A two-hour guided walk through downtown Prescott with guides who know the streets and the folk who shaped them. Territorial capital tales, Whiskey Row lore, and the buildings that outlived them all. | Flashback — LIVE at Whiskey River Tavern — 1 PM at 214 S. Montezuma St. A retro and classic cover band keeps the afternoon singing and dancing. Come for the sing-along crowd; bring your best air guitar. | La Posada – Stage to Screen — 3 PM at the Prescott Elks Theater, 117 E Gurley St. Missed the stage production? See it on screen with archival photographs tracing the history. A quiet, lovely way to spend a stormy afternoon.

[week Monday, Oct. 12] Open Mic Night: Music with a Purpose — 4 PM at THAT Brewery & Pub, 3270 N Hwy 87, Pine. The community open mic in the pines where every donation gives back locally. Bring an instrument or just your voice; the forest provides the acoustics. | Mud Run, Schnebly Hill — Noon start at the bottom of Schnebly Hill near Sedona. A rowdy off-road run up the famous red-rock route. Spectators welcome at the base; runners should bring their bravest boots.

[week Tuesday, Oct. 13] Trail Day Volunteer Build — 7 AM at Hwy 87, Pine. Pine-Strawberry Fuel Reduction calls hikers, bikers, and runners to build trail — "don't just use the trail, help build it." Gloves, water, and stout boots; breakfast of champions optional but recommended.

[week Wednesday, Oct. 14] Willow Lake Guided Walk — 3 PM. An easy walk around Willow Lake's south side with wildlife expert Walt Anderson and butterfly enthusiast Becky Hardy. Sturdy shoes and layered dress; the cottonwoods are turning. Also that day: the Willow Lake Management Plan open house, 4–6 PM at the Phippen Museum.

[week Thursday, Oct. 15] A Band Called Honalee — 7 PM, Payson High School Auditorium, 301 S. McLane Rd. A folk trio reliving Peter, Paul & Mary — "Leaving on a Jet Plane," "Blowin' in the Wind," "Puff the Magic Dragon" — plus Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and the Mamas & the Papas. An evening of harmony under the auditorium lights. | Gary Allan — 7:30 PM, Findlay Toyota Center, 3201 N. Main Street, Prescott Valley. The country headliner takes the stage with a special guest. Tickets moving; worth the drive down the mountain for the faithful.

[week Friday, Oct. 16] 3rd Friday Art Walk — 4–6 PM on Main Street, Camp Verde. Galleries and shops open their doors for a free evening stroll. Meet the makers, sip something warm, and watch the street turn gallery. | ARToberFest — Friday through Sunday at the Mazatzal Casino Event Center. The Payson Art League's annual fine art and fine craft show and sale, with the Payson Jazz Trio and an art raffle benefiting local school art programs. The Hold's artists, all in one hall.

[merchant name] Scoops Ice Cream & Espresso

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] A full espresso bar and ice-cream parlor on historic Main Street — fresh-roasted organic coffee, lattes, mochas, and cappuccinos alongside 24 flavors of Blue Bell ice cream, shakes, sundaes, and homemade pastries. Free Wi-Fi, chalk tables, and board games make it a proper lingering spot, and the kids' activity area keeps the smallfolk content. The Butterbeer Latte — two shots of almond, two of vanilla — arrives like a tankard of sweet tavern mead, foam on top: close enough to a mead-hall pour to fool a Nord, and you'll want to order a second.

[merchant review] Really nice folks here. The hot caramel brulee was tasty for sure with enough kick in a medium to fuel me back to Phoenix.

[merchant review_src] Google review (via Trustfeed)

[merchant why] The coziest cup on Main Street — espresso and ice cream under one roof, in the sweet shop the bards call Payson's best.

[merchant visit] 201 W Main St, Suite H, Payson. Mon–Thu 7 AM–8 PM, Fri 7 AM–9 PM, Sat 8 AM–9 PM, Sun 10 AM–8 PM (listings disagree on Sundays — call ahead). (928) 474-3957. Easy on the coin purse: hand-dipped shakes $2.85–$4.25.

[merchant image caption] A frothy pour at Scoops — close enough to a mead-hall pour to fool a Nord.

[due soon] The shield must rise by Saturday — but the torches, long overdue, claim first right.

[quest caption] Sconces, torches, and the Hearth shield — the craft board awaits its smith.

[tale title] The Pie-Dish Regatta

[tale] The storm had turned the Hearth's clearing into a lake, and Gus (a friendly orc with a baker's soul) was having thoughts.

"The pond reaches the porch," he announced, holding his warmest apple pie over his head, "and my pies must reach the porch people. So the pies must sail."

Before Mabel (a wood elf) could finish saying "Gus, no—", he had launched his biggest copper pie dish onto the flood like a raft and climbed aboard, pie held aloft.

Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon), delighted, seized the tow rope in his claws and flapped skyward — which, with his kinked tail, meant a zigzag course straight at the porch, then away from it, then sideways.

"Port! Starboard! No, the OTHER port!" shouted Mabel from the dry porch, waving her arms like a harbormaster.

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) waded in cheering, and Henny (the Hearth's plump Skyrim-style chicken) perched on the dish's rim like a figurehead, serene as a duchess.

Earl (an elk), dignified and dry beneath the pines, declined to participate. The sky declined to notice. One Flurry loop later, a wave crested the pie dish and crowned Earl's antlers — and the only dry thing in the clearing was the pie, which Gus delivered to the porch without spilling a crumb.

[tale image caption] Gus sails his pie-dish raft across the flooded clearing, Flurry at the tow rope.

[council] The Payson Town Council holds its regular meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 14, at 4:00 PM in the Town Hall Council Chambers, 303 N Beeline Hwy. The agenda packet had not yet been posted when this edition went to press — the town posts agendas at least 24 hours ahead, so the packet should appear by Tuesday.
Watch for it at the town's meetings & agendas page, where agendas, minutes, and the meeting recording are posted as they become available. Council normally gathers at 4:00 PM on the 2nd and 4th Wednesdays.

[headline] Thunder on the Rim: The Big Show Rolls Into Green Valley Park

[dateline] Saturday, October 10, 2026

[lead] Hail, traveler, and lend the morning sky your ear — the Rim wakes with thunder in its throat and a grand day in its parks. PAYSON — the thirty-third Beeline Cruise-In Classic Car Show rolls into Green Valley Park this morning, classics and rat rods on the grass from 8 AM to 3 PM, with the town's own Payson Days celebration — live music, vendors, and fireworks — to close the night, storms permitting. Camp Verde answers with drum and cannon for the seventieth Fort Verde Days, Sedona crams an arts festival, a blues festival, and warbirds into a single Saturday, and the school mountain-bike championships race the rain. Read on — and mind the flood watch: it runs from 11 AM through Monday morning.

[hero_caption] The thirty-third Beeline Cruise-In turns Green Valley Park into a fair of gleaming horse-drawn caravans — storm clouds be damned.

[weather] Isolated thunderstorms high 72 low 58 rain 30% day, 90% night sunrise 6:27 AM sunset 5:57 PM tomorrow Thunderstorms, 62/54

[weather_caption] Gandy flat-out refuses the storm; Maevy conducts the rain on the railing.

[weather_overheard] Overheard Last Night — A soaked traveler asked the barkeep whether the Dragonborn could not simply shout the storm aside. The barkeep only shrugged: “Aye — he shouted this morning. The thunder was just answering back.”

[today Payson] 33rd Annual Beeline Cruise-In Classic Car Show — 8 AM–3 PM, Green Valley Park, 600 S Green Valley Pkwy. The Beeline Cruisers Motor Club's thirty-third annual show: classic cars, trucks, lowriders, and rat rods — every one 25 years or older — lined up on the park grass for Best of Show and a wagon-load of category awards. Food vendors, entertainment, and raffles raising money for local charities, all free to the public. (The Friday pre-show cruise through central Payson already rolled yesterday afternoon.) | Payson Days Celebration — follows the car show at Green Valley Park. The town's own annual celebration keeps the fair going with live performances, a variety of food and vendor booths, and a fireworks display to close the night — storms permitting. Free admission, and the whole Hold comes out for it. | ACA Race #3 — Ubuntu Trail — Payson Event Center. The Arizona Cycling Association's interscholastic mountain-bike series hits the purpose-built singletrack: middle and high school riders from across the state, all in one stormy day. The organizer moved both conferences' racing to Saturday in short-track format (roughly 8 AM–3 PM, awards at 3) — Sunday racing is off.

[today Camp Verde] 70th Annual Fort Verde Days — Parade steps off at 10 AM down Main Street (finishing at the General Crook turnoff), this year's theme “America 250” with Grand Marshal Bob Weir. The festival on the town grounds at Main & Hollamon runs 11 AM–7 PM: food and craft vendors, live music, and contests. At Fort Verde State Historic Park: flag-raising and -lowering ceremonies, artillery demonstrations, living-history reenactors, Dutch-oven cooking, and military drills — free park admission all weekend. | Verde Valley Archaeology Center Indigenous Peoples Day Celebration — 10 AM–4 PM, 460 W. Finnie Flat Road. A free-admission day honoring Native American heritage: a Native American Artist Market with 30+ artists (fine art, weaving, pottery, jewelry, katsinas, silversmith work, apparel, crafts), homemade fry bread for purchase, and a noon talk by master Zuni carver Clive J. Hustito on Zuni fetishes — their symbolism and meaning — with a complimentary reception after. Note: the parade briefly closes part of Finnie Flat Road; the museum stays reachable through the Bashas' plaza entrance.

[today Sedona] 35th Annual Sedona Arts Festival — 9 AM–5 PM, Sedona Red Rock High School, 995 Upper Red Rock Loop Rd. Sedona's oldest and largest fine-arts event: 100+ juried artists from across the country showing glass, painting, metal, woodworking, photography, and ceramics, plus live music, food trucks, a beer & wine garden, and a Gourmet Row of locally made kitchen and home goods. A $15 pass covers both days; children 12 and under free with a paying adult. | Sedona Airport Wings & Wheels 2026 — 9 AM–4 PM at the Sedona Airport (up Airport Road to Tabletop Mesa). Classic cars meet classic aircraft: T-34s, T-28s, F-35 formation flybys after lunchtime, a simulated fire water drop, and the centerpiece Consolidated PB4Y-2 “Privateer” — the world's only airworthy one. Admission is a $2 donation or a nonperishable food item, every bit of it going to the Sedona Community Food Bank. | 6th Annual Sedona Red Rockin' Blues Festival — gates 11:30 AM, show noon–5 PM, Posse Grounds Pavilion, 525 Posse Ground Rd. The Northern Arizona Blues Alliance serves up local and regional Arizona blues talent — nearly all Arizona Blues Hall of Fame inductees — on the grass under the red rocks. $25 wristbands at the gate (cash only) cover the whole day of come-and-go; bring folding chairs, coolers (no alcohol), and sunblock; leashed dogs welcome.

[today Prescott] Prescott Antique Show & Vintage Market — 8 AM–3 PM, Prescott Rodeo Grounds, 840 Rodeo Dr. 50+ antique dealers from Arizona and the surrounding states: Western collectibles, Victorian antiques, mid-century furniture, vintage toys, and Native American jewelry. $10 general admission; every cent of proceeds goes to historic preservation, restoration, and education. Presented by the Thumb Butte & Yavapai Questers. | R.O.C.K. in the USA — The Music of John Mellencamp — 7:00–9:30 PM, Prescott Elks Theater, 117 E Gurley St. A high-energy tribute to Rock & Roll Hall of Famer John Mellencamp's five decades of heartland rock hits — the small-town anthems that practically wrote themselves for this Hold. Tickets run about $41–53. | Music on the Green — 4–7 PM, Prescott Valley. A free outdoor concert under the open sky with The Offbeats, a high-energy punk rock cover band tearing through Foo Fighters, Paramore, and Audioslave. Pack a blanket, grab the Valley Dwellers, and close out the afternoon loud.

[week Sun, Oct. 11] 70th Annual Fort Verde Days — day two in Camp Verde. The festival grounds at Main & Hollamon run 11 AM–4 PM, and Fort Verde State Historic Park keeps free admission 10 AM–4 PM — flag ceremonies, reenactors, and Dutch-oven demos. The Little Britches and Little Petticoats frontier-costume contest parades the littlest ones at 11 AM in the Seating Tent. | 35th Annual Sedona Arts Festival — day two, 10 AM–4 PM at Sedona Red Rock High School. Your $15 Saturday pass covers Sunday too: 100+ juried artists, live music, food trucks, and the beer & wine garden, all with the red rocks standing watch.

[week Wed, Oct. 14] Payson Town Council — regular meeting 4:00 PM in the Town Council Chambers at Town Hall, 303 N Beeline Hwy. Agendas post at least 24 hours ahead, so headline items should appear around Oct. 13 on the town's meetings page. Meetings also stream live on the town's YouTube channel. | Willow Lake Guided Walk & Open House — Prescott. A 3 PM easy walk around the south side of Willow Lake with wildlife expert Walt Anderson and butterfly enthusiast Becky Hardy (sturdy shoes, dress in layers), followed by the Willow Lake Community Open House 4–6 PM at the Phippen Museum — displays and city staff on hand, drop in anytime.

[week Thu, Oct. 15] Gary Allan — 7:30 PM, Findlay Toyota Center, 3201 N Main St, Prescott Valley. The country star brings his arena show to the Hold on a tour stop between Tacoma and Chandler. Tickets through Ticketmaster.

[week Fri, Oct. 16] Sedona Plein Air Festival begins (runs Oct 16–24) — 22nd year: 26 festival artists painting the red-rock landscape outdoors in real time, based at the Sedona Arts Center with painting sites across Sedona and the Verde Valley. Free artist demos (Oct 17 at the Outbound Sedona Hotel, 10 AM–noon; Oct 20 at the Arts Center, 1–3 PM), ticketed evening paint-outs, an awards night Oct 23, and a closing art sale Oct 24. | Fest of Fall Pickleball Rally begins (Oct 16–18) — Posse Ground Park, Sedona. The City of Sedona Parks & Rec tournament kicks off the fall festivities; the main Fest of Fall itself lands just outside this window on Saturday, Oct 17 (noon–6 PM, food trucks, vendors, cornhole, kids' zone, music).

[merchant name] Kendra's Country Bakery

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] A homegrown bakehouse on the Beeline turning out made-from-scratch cakes, cupcakes, cookies, and their famous bubble waffles. Kendra and Maureen are the edible-art duo behind some of Rim Country's most talked-about wedding cakes. The little storefront smells like butter and vanilla from the sidewalk.

[merchant review] Everything is delicious, best bubble waffles in the world!

[merchant review_src] a Restaurantji review

[merchant why] A sweet stop after thrifting Main Street — and proof that nobody guards a sweet roll like this bakery.

[merchant visit] 614 N Beeline Hwy, Payson — (928) 478-4696 — Wed–Fri 10–5, Sat–Sun 10–4 (call ahead; hours can vary) — prices moderate

[merchant image caption] Kendra's Country Bakery: where celebration cakes rise like mead-hall legends.

[quest] Finish & install the torches Overdue since Saturday — paint them faux wrought iron, UV-seal, and get them glowing.

[quest] Print the torch sconces Overdue since Oct 3 — two torches plus the socket test piece, and test-fit before the finish coats.

[quest] Design & prep the torch sconces Overdue since Sept 26 — measure the flame bulbs and sockets, find or design the model.

[quest] Build the Mogollon's Hearth shield Due Oct 17 — finalize the size for the front-door placement before cutting.

[due soon] Overdue and due today: the torches! Print them, paint them, hang them before the storm rolls in.

[tale title] The Storm-Welcome Service

[tale] With thunderstorms rumbling off the Rim, Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) declared the Hold's guests deserved a proper stormy-day greeting. So he set up his welcome station on the Hearth's front deck with a bundle of pine-bough parasols he'd lashed together himself.

The idea was sound. The parasols — being pine boughs — were enormous, fragrant, and utterly at the mercy of the wind. Every gust snatched one clean out of Jethro's hands and sent it cartwheeling across the deck. Henny the chicken took cover under the eaves and clucked advice nobody asked for.

Earl the elk, ever dignified, volunteered to hold the welcome banner in his antlers so it wouldn't blow away. But every gust caught the banner's loose end and slapped it smartly across Earl's muzzle, and each time he bowed a little deeper — as though saying, “you're welcome.”

Finally Mabel the wood elf herded the whole soaked crew inside for warm bread and cider, sighing like it was her job — which, in this forest, it is. “Best welcome ever,” the dripping guests declared. Jethro beamed. “Same time next storm?”

[tale image caption] Jethro hands out pine-bough parasols while Earl keeps the banner aloft.

[tale title] The Great Sage Freeze

[tale] Mabel (a wood elf) had a plan: winter is coming, her sage must be dried, and Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) is the Hold’s walking icebox. So on a drizzly morning she enlisted him to freeze-dry the whole harvest — a slow, careful breath, no zigzags, no funny business.

Flurry drew himself up tall, took aim at the sage bundles hanging from her garden trellis, and breathed out the steadiest, proudest ice-mist of his young life. The sage froze to perfection, glittering like diamonds on a Nord shield.

That was when Henny (the Hearth’s chicken), mid-beetle-chase, skidded through the garden at full waddle and slid, feathers and all, across the wet grass — straight into Flurry’s ice-mist. She emerged glazed like a pastry, froze mid-step, and then, unbothered professional that she is, caught her reflection in a frozen puddle and began to preen.

Mabel sighed the sigh of the only responsible adult in the forest. Gus, arriving with an empty pie dish, took one look, broke off a leaf of ice-sage, tasted it, and declared it “minty.”

The Hold’s first frost-dried herbs. Mabel calls it a disaster. The mead hall calls it seasoning.

[tale image caption] The great sage freeze — Flurry’s steadiest breath yet.

[tale title] Earl’s Shade Parlor

[tale] Middas dawned hot — the pines hummed and the porch boards popped like knuckles. By noon, Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) had opened Earl’s Shade Parlor: one pinecone buys a seat on the picnic blanket in Earl’s (an elk) long, cool shadow. Earl stood very straight and pretended the scheme was his idea. Henny (a chicken) claimed the front seat like she’d reserved weeks ago.

Business was brisk. But shadows, as Mabel (a wood elf) noted over her basket of basil, are notorious wanderers. By one o’clock the blanket sat in blazing sun, with Henny glaring at it. “New location!” Jethro announced, hauling blanket, basket, and chicken twenty paces east to the shadow’s new address. By three, half the clearing trailed Earl in a solemn procession, picnicking in motion, and Henny rode the blanket like a raft, declaring it “shadow-surfing.”

Earl accepted two red apples as tribute and stood a little straighter. Nobody has ever seen him prouder.

[tale image caption] One pinecone buys a seat in the coolest shadow in the Hold.

[tale title] The Pie-Pan Chimes of Mogollon’s Hearth

[tale] That dang ol’ Jethro was at it again Monday morning, convinced the Hearth’s front door lacked a proper greeting. Spying Gus’s (the orc baker) dented copper pie pans cooling by the tavern kitchen, he tied them in a row from the carved tavern sign with twine, grinning like the whole thing was a fine idea.

It wasn’t. The breeze coming off the pines struck up a racket like a marching band falling down a staircase, and Earl (the elk) planted himself under the sign with his great antlers tilted back, suffering in silence the way only Earl can.

Then Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) — perched on the signpost to watch the chaos — let out a tremendous sneeze, and a fine ice-mist glazed every pan. The next gust struck the frosted pans and they rang out clear and sweet as temple bells.

Mabel (the wood elf) came out of her herb garden fully prepared to be furious, stood there a long moment, and finally sighed. “Well,” she said, “they’re no worse than the warbler.”

By sundown every guest crossing the deck was giving the pans a tap on the way past. Jethro beamed. Somebody had to tell him: the Hearth already had its bells all along.

[tale image caption] Jethro’s pie-pan chimes ring clear over the Hearth’s deck.

[tale title] The Sunbeam Coronation

[tale] Earl (an elk with enormous antlers) takes his dignity seriously, and this fine sunny morning he took it straight to the Hearth’s front deck, where one perfect sunbeam lay across the planks like a warm rug. He lowered himself into it with great ceremony, folded his legs, and announced that he would be napping, and was not to be disturbed.

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) took this as an invitation to help. He fetched a pine bough to fan the great napping elk — “for the flies,” he said proudly — and waved it so enthusiastically that the first pine cone dropped straight onto Earl’s nose.

Earl did not move. Dignity, he has always maintained, is staying put.

The second cone bounced off one antler. The third landed in the crook of the other and stayed there, like a small brown crown.

Mabel (a wood elf) came out with the washing, took one look, and said what everyone was thinking: “Well. It suits him.”

Earl opened one eye, considered the crown, and went back to sleep. Some nappers get pine needles. Earl got a coronation.

[tale image caption] Earl naps on, unmoved — even a pine-cone crown cannot disturb his dignity.

No council meeting is scheduled in the next seven days; the next regular meeting is Wednesday, Oct. 14, at 4:00 PM in the Town Council Chambers, 303 N Beeline Highway. The headline item: the council heard a new Main Street proposal from Jim Hammett of White Mountain Advisory, a Show Low-based consulting firm — the only firm to answer Payson's request for proposals to update years of Main Street master plans. The pitch would turn long-struggling Main Street into an arts, cultural and business center: an arts district with a walkable commercial district, tourism draws, and a connection to a rebuilt event center, American Gulch, and the proposed Green Valley Parkway extension. The corridor would run from the Sawmill shopping center on Highway 87 to Green Valley Park, with room for musicians, artists, festivals and youth programs beside a business district built to generate sales-tax revenue. Hammett told the council the difference this time is political and community will, and that the firm would research each step with the community before projects advance. Read the full story in the Payson Roundup (Sept. 22, by Peter Aleshire). The council did not vote on the proposal. Town staff will keep working with the consultants to refine the plan and develop a price estimate; Town Manager Darren Coldwell said the council would see the consultants two or three more times before any decision. Members applauded the presentation and noted the town's groundwork — key parcel acquisitions, nearly complete flood-control engineering for American Gulch, and parallel event-center plans. The meeting's recording is on the town's YouTube channel; the written agenda and minutes were not yet posted when we went to press. In a town called Helgen, the lawbreakers were lined up for the axe — a hooded prisoner among them — when the sky went black and something roared overhead. The rider swears, hand on his heart, that it was a DRAGON. The Hold gathered by the lodge in a proper fright. A dragon! In our skies! Folks were white as Gus's flour — until somebody, and the name is lost to history, let loose a truly enormous fart, and the whole scary moment passed in a gale of laughter. The Hold stares skyward at Helgen's word — while the Dragonborn vanishes down the road. Everyone blamed Earl on the spot. Now Earl was three pine-stands away picking berries at the time, and he is DEEPLY, dignifiedly offended. Gus, meanwhile, has gone suspiciously quiet about where exactly he was standing. Nobody admits a thing. Accusations are flying. The true culprit stays anonymous. Forever. And the hooded prisoner? "Gone," the rider says. "Walked out of the dust and the shouting" — and here the rider went pale and would not finish the sentence. He was here not ten minutes ago, the Dragonborn was, the bards say. And now he's gone. T ales froM The T reeline T he l iving h aT r ack That dang ol' Jethro is at it again. It started when Earl dozed off beside the woodpile, minding his own noble business, and Jethro had himself a revelation: those enormous antlers, he declared (loudly, to nobody), would make the finest hat rack the forest has ever seen. Earl woke to find Gus's flour-dusted baker's cap looped on one tine and Mabel's sunbonnet — Mabel's! she had only set it down for half a second — dangling from another. Jethro, beaming, was lining Flurry's bottle-cap collection along the brow tines like a row of tiny goblets. Earl, dignity intact, wearing the neighborhood's hats. Earl looked at Jethro. Then, with tremendous dignity, he froze mid-step and decided to simply not move, on the theory that the nonsense would pass. It did not pass. Gus arrived with a fresh pie, saw his own hat on an elk, and dropped the pie loudly — as he does. Henny, unbothered, began pecking at it with professional interest. Flurry landed sideways in the leaf litter and pretended he meant to. Mabel sighed like it was her job, collected her bonnet, and declared Earl "the only piece of furniture in this forest that judges you back." An hour later Earl sneezed. Everything slid. Jethro caught an upside-down pie tin on his own head and declared the rack a triumph. Earl stalked off into the pines, dignified, one pie tin still hooked on an antler, which he refused to acknowledge for the rest of the day. T ales froM The T reeline T he P ies T haT W ouldn ’ T b udge Gus sets his berry pies on the tavern windowsill every Saturday to cool, and every Saturday the whole forest knows better than to touch them. Every Saturday except this one. Flurry was only trying to help. “Just a breath,” he said, all big-eyed and earnest, and gave those pies the tiniest puff of his ice-breath. The pies froze to the sill. Not frosted — welded. Gus tapped one with a knuckle and it rang like a dinner bell. “Oh no,” Gus whispered, which for Gus is practically shouting. Jethro parades the windowsill — pies and all — while Gus gives chase. Now, Jethro does not always think things through, but Jethro has shoulders like oak beams and a heart to match. “Stand back,” he said, wrapped those enormous arms around the windowsill, and pulled. The sill came with him. So did the pies. So did a fair piece of the tavern wall’s dignity. He paraded through the clearing holding the whole windowsill over his head like a trophy, pies and all, grinning that big Mogollon grin, while Gus chased after him wailing, “My sill! My pies! My Saturday!” Earl watched from the woodpile with enormous dignity and said nothing, which said everything. Mabel thawed the pies with warm towels and declared them, quote, “structurally improved.” Printed with pride in Payson, in the shadow of the Rim · Set in hot metal by Dude, Bard of the Morning Scroll · May your Saturday be free of dragons, Clay.

[headline] Two Fairs, One Hold: Fair Week Rides Into Payson

[dateline] Wednesday, September 30, 2026

[lead] HAIL, wayfarers, and welcome to the Hearth! The pines stand gold-tipped in the morning light, the chicken has donned her galoshes against an afternoon shower, and Payson braces for the grandest double-header of the season — two fairs in one Hold, four days of rodeo dust and Highland revelry. One more bit of news for the regulars: this Scroll now keeps its dates by the old Tamrielic reckoning — the bards’ proper calendar — with the lowlanders’ dates riding alongside so no traveler misses a thing; we stand at the close of Hearthfire (the lowlanders call it “September” — odd name for a month that smells of pine smoke!), with Frostfall but two days hence. By the Nine, it’s a fine week to be in Rim Country.

[hero_caption] Two fairs, one Hold: the North Inch Highland village and the County Fair’s rodeo grounds beneath the Mogollon Rim.

[weather] PM showers high 65 low 50 rain 30% sunrise 6:19 AM sunset 6:10 PM tomorrow Sunny, 80/55

[weather_caption] The Hearth’s chicken, dancing in the afternoon rain — galoshes on, umbrella up.

[weather_overheard] Overheard at the Mead Hall Last Night — A traveler shook his fist at the rain and shouted “Clear Skies!” The barkeep just shrugged: “The Dragonborn was here not ten minutes ago — and the clouds near broke for him.”

[today Payson] Morning at the Library — Qi Gong 9 AM, Baby Story Time 10:30 AM, Tai Chi 11:30 AM, Payson Public Library, 328 N McLane Rd — monthly calendar | Bible Study at Juanita’s — 9–10 AM, 139 Hash Knife Drive — details

[today Camp Verde] Online Safety & Security — 4–6 PM, Camp Verde Community Library, 130 N Black Bridge Rd; free hands-on class, bring thy device — details | Common Cause Training — 5–7 PM, Terracotta Room, Camp Verde Community Library — library calendar

[today Show Low] BINGO! — 3 PM, Pinetop-Lakeside — 1594 Johnson Drive; 15 games, $15 buy-in, open to the public — details

[today Prescott] Musicians with Heart Open Mic — 7–10 PM, Jersey Lilly Saloon; donations go to the Yavapai County Food Bank — details

[week Fredas, 2nd of Frostfall (Oct. 2)] First Friday in the Galleries — Sedona’s monthly art evening runs 4–7 PM at Tlaquepaque Arts & Shopping Village, 336 AZ-179. Gallery receptions, live music, and wine tastings, with the artists themselves on hand to talk about their work. A fine evening stroll as the Valley Dwellers trade the lowland heat for red-rock air. details

[week Loredas, 3rd of Frostfall (Oct. 3)] 42nd Folk Music Festival — the festival returns to the Sharlot Hall Museum, 415 W Gurley St, Prescott after a seven-year rest, Saturday 9 AM–5 PM. More than 50 musicians across four stages, food trucks, a new Kid Zone, and a “Folk Fest Feast” area; admission $15, kids 9 and under free — bring lawn chairs. Friday evening offers a limited-seating Folk Legacy Trio concert, 6–9 PM. details | Pine-Strawberry Fall Festival & October Craft Show — the Pine Strawberry Business Community fills the community center ramada, 3886 N Highway 87, Pine, with handcrafts, Saturday 8 AM–5 PM and Sunday 8 AM–4 PM. Pumpkin patch and hayrides round out the fall tradition; grounds are alcohol- and smoke-free. details | Twice Nice Fall Thrifty — the thrift shop, 527 S Main St, Camp Verde, hosts raffles and prizes for donated items, food trucks, and a live radio broadcast, 10 AM–2 PM. Sister duo Kaleidoscope Redrocks plays live noon–2, donating every tip to the Verde Valley Sanctuary. details | Verde Valley Farmers Market — the market closes its 2026 season Saturday, 8–11 AM at 75 E Hollamon St, Camp Verde. One last morning of fresh local produce before the stalls sleep till spring — arrive hungry.

[week Tirdas, 6th of Frostfall (Oct. 6)] Trail Day Volunteer Build — lend thy back to the PINE Strawberry Fuel Reduction crew, Tuesday 7 AM–noon, off Highway 87 just before Pine. Volunteers clear brush, move rocks, and shape new community trails; tools provided — bring water, sunscreen, gloves, and work shoes, and RSVP trails@psfuelreduction.org. details

[featured kicker] Fair Week in the Hold

[featured title] Two Fairs, One Hold

[featured text] The North Inch Renaissance Faire holds its maiden voyage on the Payson Golf Course, 1504 W Country Club Dr, Friday 9 AM–5 PM, Saturday 9 AM–9 PM, Sunday 9 AM–5 PM. A Scottish village rises on the fairways: artisans, combat demonstrations, axe throwing and archery, the Clan Armstrong fire-dancing show, the Queen of Scots’ court, the Pirate Queen Scarlett McBayne, and the Queen of the Faeries. (A stranger came through town yesterday holding a queer device before him that wailed like a heartbroken mammoth and never once ran out of breath — a clever wind-spell doing the breathing for him. Other travelers have called it a “bagpipie.”)  Meanwhile the 72nd Annual Northern Gila County Fair & B.U.C.K.L.E. Festival holds court at the Payson Event Center, 1400 S Beeline Hwy, Thursday through Saturday. Professional bull riding, ranch rodeo, barrel racing, goat roping, mutton bustin’, livestock shows and the Junior Livestock Auction, the Arizona State Fiddle Festival, live music, mini-carnival rides, and vendors — with Thursday evening’s opening ceremony “Hailing Our Heroes” honoring veterans and hometown heroes.

[featured details] North Inch: $8 adults, $4 children, active-duty military free — see northinchrf.com. County Fair: $3–$5 admission, $5 parking — tickets via BAMM.

[featured why] Two fairs, one Hold, and a weekend thy guests will talk about all winter — send them Friday for the jousts and Saturday for the bulls, and they’ll owe thee a mug of mead.

[featured image caption] The North Inch faire raises its banners for the first time.

[merchant name] BoSa Donuts

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] BoSa Donuts is a walk-in donut shop and bakery where the donuts are made fresh daily from scratch. The case holds the classics — glazed, chocolate iced, maple long johns, apple fritters, cinnamon twists, bear claws, and donut holes — plus breakfast sandwiches like sausage, egg & cheese on a croissant, coffee, cappuccino, and smoothies. Quick service with dine-in or drive-through, and the apple fritter is the thing the regulars swear by.

[merchant review] Excellent donuts. The Apple Fritter was my absolute favorite. Crispy, crunchy glaze on the outside with perfectly cooked apples inside.

[merchant review_src] TripAdvisor review

[merchant why] BoSa’s apple fritter is the Hold’s own sweet roll — and these come fresh daily with no guard in sight to confiscate them. A cheap, cheerful morning break along the Beeline, right as the Valley Dwellers roll into town for fair week.

[merchant visit] 303 S Beeline Hwy, Payson, AZ 85541 — open daily from 5 AM; (928) 474-8889; $ inexpensive; drive-through, and the case is fullest in the morning.

[merchant image caption] Sweet rolls, fresh daily — the Hold’s answer to the guards’ favorite.

[quest] Print the torch sconces Due Saturday, Oct. 3 — print two torches plus the socket test piece; test-fit the bulb and socket first.

[due soon] The sconce design is overdue and the printing must fire by Saturday — the Hearth’s torchlight waits on thee.

[quest caption] The craftsman at his bench, where the Hearth’s torch sconces take shape.

[tale title] Flurry Gilds the Rain

[tale] It rained on Middas afternoon, the soft gray kind, and Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) took it as a personal invitation.  Nobody’s quite sure whose idea it was — Henny (the Hearth’s plump chicken) claims she only mentioned the rain looked “a mite plain” — but by mid-afternoon Flurry was perched on the Hearth’s front deck, exhaling his finest ice-mist into the drizzle, gilding every falling drop into a tiny glittering jewel.  “I am gilding the rain,” he announced grandly, then landed sideways in a rain barrel for emphasis.  By the time Gus (a friendly orc with a baker’s soul) came out with a tray of honey cakes, the whole deck sparkled like a kicked-over treasure chest. He took one step, skidded clean across the jewel-ice, and landed sitting down with the tray held high overhead — not one crumb lost.  “Save the cakes!” he bellowed, which is how Gus says “I’m fine.”  Mabel (a wood elf with the patience of a saint) surveyed the glittering deck, the dragon in the rain barrel, and the orc on his backside, and declared Flurry the Hold’s first official weathermage.  Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) has already asked whether the weathermage can gild his bathwater. Mabel said no.

[tale image caption] The deck, gilded; Gus, grounded; the cakes, miraculously airborne.

[headline] Fair Week: County Fair Opens, a Faire Village at the Golf Course

[dateline] Thursday, October 1, 2026

[lead] HAIL, fair-wayfarers, and a bright good morning to thee! Frostfall (the lowlanders — our Valley Dwellers up from the southern vale — call it “October”, a mouthful of a name for a month that smells of pine and kettle corn!) opens with a clear sky, a sun-warmed deck, and the biggest weekend of the year: the 72nd Annual Northern Gila County Fair throws its gates wide today at the Payson Event Center, and tomorrow the North Inch Renaissance Faire raises a Scottish village on the Payson Golf Course fairways. Bulls, bagpipes, fiddles, and funnel cake — by the Nine, Rim Country has outdone itself. Below: what’s on today in every Hold, the days ahead, the Hearth’s own quests, and a diner where the iron drakes come home to roost.

[hero_caption] Fair week beneath the Rim: the County Fair’s rodeo grounds and the Highland village, side by side.

[weather] Sunny high 79 low 56 rain 0% sunrise 6:20 AM sunset 6:09 PM tomorrow Sunny, 81/54

[weather_caption] The Hearth’s chicken, basking in the Frostfall sun — one wing up for shade.

[weather_overheard] Overheard at the Mead Hall Last Night — A fair-goer swears something tall and hairy stood in the pines above the grounds, counting the pies on the bake-table — twice, careful as a tax man. The barkeep only shrugged: “Aye. Even the woods come down for fair week.”

[today Payson] 72nd Annual Northern Gila County Fair & B.U.C.K.L.E. Festival — opens 9 AM, Payson Event Center, 1400 S Beeline Hwy; opening ceremony “Hailing Our Heroes” this evening, Rim Country plays 7:30 PM | Morning at the Library — Let’s Talk Spanish 9 AM, Toddler Time 10:30 AM, Line Dancing 1:45 PM, Payson Public Library, 328 N McLane Rd — monthly calendar | Rumsey Park Battle — disc golf league round, 4:15–6:30 PM, Rumsey Park Disc Golf Course

[today Camp Verde] Citizenship Class — 6–7:30 PM, Camp Verde Community Library, 130 Black Bridge Rd; free weekly class, call (928) 554-8398

[today Sedona] Sedona Yoga Festival — opening day, from 12 PM, Outbound Sedona, 1752 AZ-179; runs through Sunday | Hillside Morning Soundbath — 10 AM, 671 AZ-179; alchemy crystal singing bowls, $44

[today Prescott] Perfect Poise AZ Cruise to the Pines — classic car gathering from 12 PM, Watson Lake, Watson Lake Park Rd

[week Fredas, 2nd of Frostfall (Fri, Oct. 2)] North Inch Renaissance Faire — the inaugural Scottish village opens 9 AM–5 PM on the Payson Golf Course, 1504 W Country Club Dr. Artisans, combat demonstrations, axe throwing and archery, the Queen of Scots’ court, and a stranger with a queer wind-spell device that wails like a heartbroken mammoth (other travelers have called it a “bagpipie”). $8 adults, $4 children, active-duty military free. | County Fair, Day Two — the fair runs on at the Payson Event Center with bull riding at 6 PM and Moonshine Mafia on stage at 8 PM. Livestock shows, the Arizona State Fiddle Festival, mini-carnival rides, and vendors all day — arrive hungry and stay for the music. | First Friday in the Galleries — Sedona’s monthly art evening runs 4–7 PM at Tlaquepaque Arts & Shopping Village, 336 AZ-179. Gallery receptions, live music, and wine tastings, with the artists themselves on hand — a fine evening stroll as the Valley Dwellers trade the lowland heat for red-rock air. | Prescott Area Artist Studio Tour — opens Friday, 10 AM–4 PM, and runs all weekend: 74 artists across 52 private studios and three art centers, free and self-guided. Watch the makers at their benches and take home a one-of-a-kind piece.

[week Loredas, 3rd of Frostfall (Sat, Oct. 3)] County Fair, Final Day — the 72nd Annual Northern Gila County Fair & B.U.C.K.L.E. Festival closes out Saturday at the Payson Event Center: Western Fusion Band at 2:30 PM, Kristen Merlin headlining at 8 PM, the Junior Livestock Auction, ranch rodeo, and barrel racing. One last day of dust, fiddles, and fair food — don’t let thy guests miss it. | North Inch Renaissance Faire, Day Two — the Highland village runs its longest day, 9 AM–9 PM at the Payson Golf Course. The Clan Armstrong fire-dancers, the Pirate Queen Scarlett McBayne, and the Queen of the Faeries hold court — send the Valley Dwellers up early for the jousts and let them linger past dusk. | 42nd Folk Music Festival — returns to the Sharlot Hall Museum, 415 W Gurley St, Prescott, 9 AM–5 PM after a seven-year rest. More than 50 musicians across four stages, food trucks, and a new Kid Zone; admission $15, kids 9 and under free — bring lawn chairs. | Pine-Strawberry Fall Festival & October Craft Show — handcrafts fill the community center ramada, 3886 N Highway 87, Pine, Saturday 8 AM–5 PM and Sunday 8 AM–4 PM. Pumpkin patch and hayrides round out the fall tradition; grounds are alcohol- and smoke-free. | Twice Nice Fall Thrifty & Farmers Market Finale — Camp Verde’s thrift celebration runs 10 AM–2 PM at 527 S Main St with raffles, food trucks, and live music from Kaleidoscope Redrocks, while the Verde Valley Farmers Market closes its 2026 season 8–11 AM at 75 E Hollamon St. One last morning of fresh local produce before the stalls sleep till spring.

[week Sundas, 4th of Frostfall (Sun, Oct. 4)] North Inch Renaissance Faire, Final Day — the Scottish village’s last stand runs 9 AM–5 PM at the Payson Golf Course. If thy guests have not yet seen the combat demonstrations or paid court to the Queen of Scots, Sundas is their final chance this year — haste ye back! | Sedona Community Farmers Market — Sunday 8 AM–12 PM at 2201 W State Route 89A (Wells Fargo Bank parking lot), West Sedona. Local and seasonal harvest, artisan goods, and live music — a gentle morning after a weekend of fairs.

[week Tirdas, 6th of Frostfall (Tue, Oct. 6)] Trail Day Volunteer Build — lend thy back to the PINE Strawberry Fuel Reduction crew, Tuesday 7 AM–noon, off Highway 87 just before Pine. Volunteers clear brush, move rocks, and shape new community trails; tools provided — bring water, sunscreen, gloves, and work shoes, and RSVP trails@psfuelreduction.org.

[merchant name] Crosswinds Restaurant

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] Crosswinds is the beloved diner at Payson Airport, where the windows look straight down the landing-meadow — a long mown field the lowlanders call a “runway” — and the great iron drakes, held aloft by a clever levitation spell (or so the barkeeps swear), come and go while you eat. Drake-barns line the meadow’s edge, and a striped wind-serpent (other travelers call it a “windsock”) wriggles atop its pole, sniffing the breeze for the riders, who will not stir without its counsel. The regulars add that if that truly is a sock, they have no wish to meet the giant it would fit — whether it be windy or not. All morning the valley drakes come lumbering up from the lowlands with Valley Dwellers in their bellies, bound for pie: any drake can leap off the meadow — it is the landing that tries a rider’s soul, though at Crosswinds every landing ends, happily, at breakfast. Inside: all-day breakfast — chicken-fried steak and eggs, biscuits and gravy, burgers, and homemade pies worth crossing the valley for. Try the chocolate cream pie; pilots have flown in for it for generations.

[merchant review] The food was really good but the pie...wow. The pie was amazing.

[merchant review_src] Birdeye review

[merchant why] Breakfast beside the drakes’ landing-meadow and the best pie in the Hold — send thy guests at dawn, before the fair gates open, and they’ll thank thee before the first bull bucks.

[merchant visit] 800 W Airport Rd Ste B, Payson, AZ 85541 — open daily 6 AM–3 PM (Fridays till 4 PM); (928) 474-1613; $ inexpensive; it fills up on fair-weekend mornings, so go early and ask what pies came out of the oven.

[merchant image caption] Pie first, iron drakes second — Crosswinds feeds both kinds of traveler.

[quest] Design & prep the torch sconces Overdue since Sept. 26 — measure the flame bulb and socket, then find or design the wall-torch sconce model.

[quest] Print the torch sconces Due Loredas, Oct. 3 — print two torches plus the socket test piece; test-fit the bulb and socket first.

[due soon] The sconce design is overdue and the printing must fire by Loredas — the Hearth’s torchlight waits on thee.

[quest caption] The craftsman at his bench, where the Hearth’s torch sconces take shape.

[tale title] Earl’s Laundry Service

[tale] The sun came out grand on Turdas morning, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) took one look at his dripping wash line and had what he called a notion.

“Earl,” he announced, “you’re the tallest rack in the Hold.”

Earl (an elk with enormous antlers) stood very still, which everyone took for agreement. By mid-morning his antlers wore two shirts, a row of socks, and one magnificent sheet billowing like a sail bound for Scotland, that mist-shrouded realm across the eastern sea.

Henny (the Hearth’s plump chicken) inspected the work, claimed the sunniest sock for a throne, and refused to move for anything short of corn.

It might have worked, too, if the sheet hadn’t caught a proper gust: Earl took two dignified steps sideways, wearing the whole laundry like a very embarrassed ship.

Mabel (a wood elf) sighed the sigh of a woman who has folded this exact wash before. “Next time,” she said, “we ask the elk first.”

Earl has not commented. The sheet, however, is dry.

[tale image caption] One elk, two shirts, and a sheet bound for Scotland.

[headline] North Inch Faire Opens; Bulls Ride at Dusk

[dateline] Friday, October 2, 2026

[lead] HAIL and well met, friends of the Hearth, on a golden Fredas morning! Frostfall deepens — the lowlanders call it “October”, a clanking great name for a month of pine smoke and honeyed light — and the Hold fairly hums with it: this very day the North Inch Renaissance Faire throws wide its gates, a whole Scottish village risen upon the Payson Golf Course fairways, while at the Event Center the 72nd Annual Northern Gila County Fair rides into its second day with bulls at dusk. Bagpipes by morning, bulls by evening — by the Nine, Rim Country has outdone itself. Below: what’s on today in every Hold, the days ahead, the Hearth’s own quests, a mead-hall of the Verde Valley, and word from the wider Rim.

[hero_caption] Opening day beneath the Rim: caber-tossing, axe-throwing and archery on the fairways, while a Nord rider faces the bulls by torchlight.

[weather] Sunny high 80 low 54 rain 0% sunrise 6:20 AM sunset 6:07 PM tomorrow Sunny, 82/56

[weather_caption] Henny holds court on the sun-warmed deck, daring a single cloud to show itself.

[weather_overheard] Overheard Last Night — A trapper swears the quitting horn had a second voice humming underneath it — deep as a bear in a barrel. The barkeep only shrugged: “That’s Jethro, practicing his harmonies for fair week.”

[today Payson] North Inch Renaissance Faire — opening day, 9 AM–5 PM, Payson Golf Course, 1504 W Country Club Dr. The inaugural Scottish village wakes: artisans, combat demonstrations, Highland games, axe throwing and archery, the Queen of Scots’ court, and a lone Scots piper whose queer wind-device wails like a heartbroken mammoth. $8 adults, $4 children; active-duty military free. | 72nd Annual Northern Gila County Fair — day two at the Payson Event Center, 1400 S Beeline Hwy; gates 9 AM, livestock shows and the Arizona State Fiddle Festival all day, and pro bull riding at 6 PM. Fair admission $3–$5.

[today Sedona] First Friday in the Galleries — monthly gallery receptions 4–7 PM along Gallery Row, 336 AZ-179. Meet the artists, music, wine tastings, and treats among the red rocks.

[today Show Low] 30th Annual Dave Conatser XC Invite — high-school cross-country invitational, 9–11 AM at McHood Park. | The Locals Market — weekly local market 3–7 PM at the Pinedale Public Library in Pinedale. Vendors, Gosling Ranch goods, and often a food truck.

[today Prescott] Prescott Area Artist Studio Tour — opens today; a free self-guided tour of 74 artists across 52 private studios plus three art centers, 10 AM–4 PM daily through Sunday. Watch live demonstrations, meet the artists, and buy original work. | Bees Fall Classic Car Auction — preview day from 3 PM at Pine Ridge Marketplace, 3106 Gateway Blvd; the live auction kicks off Saturday at 11 AM. Free admission and parking. | Doug Dillman, Live — live music on Whiskey Row, 7–10:30 PM at the Whiskey River Tavern, 214 S Montezuma St.

[week Loredas, 3rd of Frostfall (Sat, Oct. 3)] North Inch Renaissance Faire — the faire’s long day, 9 AM–9 PM on the Payson Golf Course fairways, 1504 W Country Club Dr. A full day of Scottish artisans, combat demonstrations, music, and storytelling in the inaugural Highland village — the one day to stay for the evening merriment. $8 adults, $4 children; active-duty military free. | Northern Gila County Fair — final day at the Payson Event Center, 1400 S Beeline Hwy; gates 9 AM and the 72nd annual fair wraps tonight about 10 PM. Pro bull riding, ranch rodeo, goat roping, the Junior Livestock Auction, and the Arizona State Champion Fiddle Festival. Admission $3–$5. | Pine-Strawberry October Craft Fair — the 36th annual fall craft fair, 8 AM–5 PM at the Pine-Strawberry Community Center Ramada, 3886 N Highway 87, Pine. Handmade goods from Rim Country crafters on smoke-free, alcohol-free grounds; continues Sunday 8 AM–4 PM. | Verde Valley Farmers Market — the final market of the 2026 season, 8–11 AM at 75 E Hollamon St, Camp Verde. The last chance this year for Verde Valley produce and local goods before the stalls close for the season. | 42nd Folk Music Festival — Sharlot Hall Museum, Prescott; gates 9 AM, music 10 AM–5 PM across the museum grounds. Local and regional acoustic musicians and dancers celebrate Prescott’s folk heritage, a tradition since 1980. $15 for non-members; members and children under 9 free.

[week Sundas, 4th of Frostfall (Sun, Oct. 4)] North Inch Renaissance Faire — final day, 9 AM–5 PM at the Payson Golf Course. The last chance to walk the inaugural Highland village before the tents come down. $8 adults, $4 children; active-duty military free. | Sedona Community Farmers Market — 8–11 AM at 2201 W SR 89A, Sedona. Local growers and makers in the red rocks; go early for the best pickings.

[week Tirdas, 6th of Frostfall (Tue, Oct. 6)] Trail Day Volunteer Build — 7 AM–noon off Highway 87 just before Pine (parking at the large circular dirt turnout). Pine-Strawberry Fuel Reduction volunteers clear brush, move rocks, and shape trails that double as fire-access routes; bring water, sunscreen, and gloves, tools provided. Email trails@psfuelreduction.org to join.

[merchant name] Verde Brewing Company

[merchant town] Camp Verde

[merchant blurb] Verde Brewing Company is an independent craft brewery and gastropub tucked into an industrial park off the beaten track in Camp Verde, pouring twelve of its own brews — no magic required, just malt, hops, and patience. The signature pour is the Wildflower Honey IPA, brewed with local wildflower honey, alongside the Smokey Rye Lager and the Gold Buckle honey lager. The kitchen keeps a family-friendly American menu built for beer — the thing to order is the elote nachos with pulled pork, heaped crisp flatbread the reviewers rave about.

[merchant review] We stopped here on our way back to Phoenix from Sedona. The brewery is a little off the beaten track but easily found. The staff were friendly and the beer was excellent. I really enjoyed the sour. Also the food was very good especially the hotdogs. Recommend a visit.

[merchant review_src] a TripAdvisor review

[merchant why] A true mead-hall of the Verde Valley — Camp Verde’s own independent brewery, where Valley Dwellers can taste the valley in a glass and carry a growler home to the Hearth.

[merchant visit] 724 N Industrial Dr, Unit 7a, Camp Verde, AZ 86322 — open daily 11 AM–9 PM; (928) 300-6724; $$ moderate; the beer garden is dog-friendly, and happy hour runs Mon–Fri 2–5 PM ($2 off pints).

[merchant image caption] The brewhouse at Verde Brewing Company, where the taps never run dry.

[quest] Print the torch sconces Due Loredas, Oct. 3 — print two torches plus the socket test piece; test-fit the bulb and socket first.

[quest] Design & prep the torch sconces Overdue since Sept. 26 — measure the flame bulb and socket, then find or design the wall-torch sconce model.

[due soon] The sconce printing must fire by Loredas, and the design sits overdue — the Hearth’s torchlight waits on thee.

[quest caption] The craftsman’s bench, where the Hearth’s torch sconces take shape — and the shield waits its turn.

[tale title] Henny’s Shiny Brood

[tale] On a sun-warmed Fredas morning, with the whole Hold smelling of pine and possibility, Henny (the Hearth’s plump Skyrim-style chicken) discovered Flurry’s hollow log.

Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) keeps his life’s treasure there: bottle caps and lost buttons, each one entered in a bark ledger as the forest’s official lost-and-found. Henny took one look at the glittering pile, fluffed herself to twice her size, and settled down in the middle of it with the air of a queen claiming a throne.

“Those are not eggs,” Flurry said, very carefully, from a safe distance.

Henny did not move. Henny tucked a particularly shiny cap a little further under her wing.

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) tried diplomacy, which mostly meant looming nearby and smiling hopefully. Mabel (a wood elf) arrived, sighed the deep sigh of a woman who has seen this exact nonsense before, and fetched a tin pie plate of warm mash.

“Trade,” Mabel announced. “One plate of mash for one log of bottle caps.”

Henny considered. Henny ate the mash. Henny stayed exactly where she was.

The lost-and-found remains closed until further notice. Flurry has started a waiting list.

[tale image caption] Henny claims Flurry’s bottle-cap hoard as her own — the lost-and-found is closed until further notice.

[headline] The Faire's Long Day; the Fair's Last Ride

[dateline] Saturday, October 3, 2026

[lead] GOOD morrow, wayfarers, and mind the sun — Loredas dawns bright as a polished septim over the Rim! Frostfall settles in proper now — the lowlanders call it "October", a name that lands like a dropped shield — and the Hold answers with the longest day of the season: the North Inch Renaissance Faire runs nine of the morning clock to nine of the evening, caber and claymore by daylight and torchlight revelry after, while the 72nd Northern Gila County Fair takes its final bow at the Event Center with bulls at dusk and fiddles ringing. Two fairs, one Hold, and no excuse to sit by the fire. Below: the day's doings in every Hold, the days ahead, the Hearth's own quests, a new Merchant of the Hold, and a tale from the treeline.

[hero_caption] The faire's long day and the county fair's last ride: caber-tossing and torchlight revelry on the fairways, bulls at dusk in the arena.

[weather] Sunny high 83 low 56 rain 1% sunrise 6:21 AM sunset 6:07 PM tomorrow Sunny, 83/57

[weather_caption] Henny basks on the sun-warmed deck, one wing raised against the glare — daring a single cloud to show itself.

[weather_overheard] Overheard Last Night — A traveler come up from the valley for fair day swears the bagpipes followed him all the way up the Beeline. The barkeep only shrugged: "Aye — they do that. They follow everybody home."

[today Payson] North Inch Renaissance Faire — the faire's long day, 9 AM–9 PM, Payson Golf Course, 1504 W Country Club Dr. Scottish artisans, combat demonstrations, Highland games, music, and evening torchlight merriment in the inaugural Highland village. $8 adults, $4 children; active-duty military free. | 72nd Annual Northern Gila County Fair — final day at the Payson Event Center, 1400 S Beeline Hwy; gates 9 AM, the fair wraps tonight about 10 PM. Pro bull riding, ranch rodeo, goat roping, the Junior Livestock Auction, and the Arizona State Champion Fiddle Festival. Admission $3–$5.

[today Pine-Strawberry] Pine-Strawberry October Craft Fair — the 36th annual fall craft fair, 8 AM–5 PM at the Pine-Strawberry Community Center Ramada, 3886 N Highway 87, Pine. Handmade goods from Rim Country crafters on smoke-free, alcohol-free grounds; continues Sunday 8 AM–4 PM. | Kilted Spirit Trio — Celtic music at noon at the Lodge at 5600, Pine — a fitting soundtrack for faire weekend among the pines.

[today Camp Verde] Verde Valley Farmers Market — the final market of the 2026 season, 8–11 AM at the town ramada, 75 E Hollamon St. The last chance this year for Verde Valley produce and local goods before the stalls close for the season. | Twice Nice Fall Thrifty — community day 10 AM–2 PM at Twice Nice Thriftique, 527 S Main St. Donation raffles, food trucks, and live music by the sister duo Kaleidoscope Redrocks, with a live radio remote.
